key_insight: LLM-as-judge bias is not just a prompt/input-output problem—it also shows up in the model’s hidden representations. The paper finds a representation-level account of bias that can explain, measure, and help mitigate unfair scoring across multiple judges and benchmarks.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the challenge of understanding why LLM judges produce biased scores, such as favoring certain inputs or styles, and moves beyond surface-level perturbation studies to identify the internal mechanisms behind these biases.
method: Analyze hidden-state geometry of judge models to see how biased and unbiased inputs are represented internally.
Evaluate seven judges across seven bias types and nine benchmarks to test whether representation-level bias patterns generalize.
Compare representation-level findings with input-output bias measurements to build a complementary mechanistic interpretability view of LLM-as-judge behavior.
impact: This helps researchers and practitioners diagnose unfairness in LLM evaluators more precisely, rather than relying only on prompt tweaks. It also opens the door to stronger mitigations that target the model’s internal decision process, improving trust in automated evaluation systems.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram of input-output bias vs. hidden-state bias
Hidden representation geometry plot showing clustered judge inputs
Flowchart of the evaluation pipeline across judges, bias types, and benchmarks
Icon-based comparison of biased vs. unbiased scoring outcomes
paper_title: Inside the Unfair Judge: A Mechanistic Interpretability Account of LLM-as-Judge Bias
paper_authors: Zixiang Xu, Sixian Li, Huaxing Liu, Xiang Wang, Shuai Li
